q:

Kennedy v. Bremerton School District

West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette

Kennedy v. Bremerton School District
West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette

Because it incorporated the Speech Clause against states

q: What did West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette hold?

o: The state, even assuming the same precautions
The worshippers, through expert testimony
No one, because risk is irrelevant to comparing
The court, by taking judicial notice of science
e: The government must show the religious activity is riskier even with the same precautions. It doesn’t matter that some secular activities are treated as badly.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Tandon v. Newsom

q: In Carson v. Makin, why wasn’t the tuition program a “public education” benefit Maine could keep secular?
o: The private schools could be selective and skip the state curriculum
Most students in the program attended religious schools anyway
Maine’s constitution forbade public funding of private schooling
The program paid parents directly rather than paying the schools
e: Participating schools could be selective, often weren’t free, didn’t follow the state curriculum, needn’t hire certified teachers, and could be single-sex.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Carson v. Makin

q: Which facts belong to Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith?
o: Native American Church members seeking an exemption from a drug ban for ritual peyote use.
A city bans ritual animal sacrifice through ordinances that exempt nearly every secular killing.
A three-household cap on at-home worship while salons and stores could exceed it.
Parents denied opt-outs from LGBTQ-inclusive storybooks in elementary English classes.
e: Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith (1990): Native American Church members seeking an exemption from a drug ban for ritual peyote use.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith

q: Which facts belong to Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah?
o: A city bans ritual animal sacrifice through ordinances that exempt nearly every secular killing.
Native American Church members seeking an exemption from a drug ban for ritual peyote use.
A city cuts off a Catholic foster care agency that won’t certify same-sex couples.
A football coach disciplined for praying quietly at midfield after games.
e: Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah (1993): A city bans ritual animal sacrifice through ordinances that exempt nearly every secular killing.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah

q: Which facts belong to Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission?
o: A baker’s religious refusal to make a same-sex wedding cake, met with commissioners’ open disparagement.
A city cuts off a Catholic foster care agency that won’t certify same-sex couples.
Native American Church members seeking an exemption from a drug ban for ritual peyote use.
A football coach disciplined for praying quietly at midfield after games.
e: Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission (2018): A baker’s religious refusal to make a same-sex wedding cake, met with commissioners’ open disparagement.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission

q: Which facts belong to Fulton v. City of Philadelphia?
o: A city cuts off a Catholic foster care agency that won’t certify same-sex couples.
A baker’s religious refusal to make a same-sex wedding cake, met with commissioners’ open disparagement.
Native American Church members seeking an exemption from a drug ban for ritual peyote use.
A state tuition program that pays only for “nonsectarian” private schools.
e: Fulton v. City of Philadelphia (2021): A city cuts off a Catholic foster care agency that won’t certify same-sex couples.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Fulton v. City of Philadelphia

q: Which facts belong to Tandon v. Newsom?
o: A three-household cap on at-home worship while salons and stores could exceed it.
A city cuts off a Catholic foster care agency that won’t certify same-sex couples.
Native American Church members seeking an exemption from a drug ban for ritual peyote use.
A state tuition program that pays only for “nonsectarian” private schools.
e: Tandon v. Newsom (2021): A three-household cap on at-home worship while salons and stores could exceed it.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Tandon v. Newsom

q: Which facts belong to Carson v. Makin?
o: A state tuition program that pays only for “nonsectarian” private schools.
A city cuts off a Catholic foster care agency that won’t certify same-sex couples.
A football coach disciplined for praying quietly at midfield after games.
Native American Church members seeking an exemption from a drug ban for ritual peyote use.
e: Carson v. Makin (2022): A state tuition program that pays only for “nonsectarian” private schools.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Carson v. Makin

q:
Which case is this from?
Strict scrutiny for every incidental burden would create “a private right to ignore generally applicable laws,” a “constitutional anomaly.”
o: Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith
Tandon v. Newsom
Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission
Mahmoud v. Taylor
e: From Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith (1990).
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith

q:
Which case is this from?
The city’s claims that secular killings were “obviously justified” were ipse dixits; society imposed on worshippers what it would not impose on itself.
o: Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah
Fulton v. City of Philadelphia
Tandon v. Newsom
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District
e: From Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah (1993).
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah

q:
Which case is this from?
Three bakers who refused cakes with messages disapproving of same-sex marriage were found to have acted lawfully.
o: Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission
Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith
Tandon v. Newsom
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District
e: From Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission (2018).
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission

q:
Which case is this from?
The question is not whether the government has a compelling interest generally, but whether it has one in denying an exemption to this claimant.
o: Fulton v. City of Philadelphia
Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith
Tandon v. Newsom
Carson v. Makin
e: From Fulton v. City of Philadelphia (2021).
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Fulton v. City of Philadelphia

q:
Which case is this from?
The state “cannot assume the worst when people go to worship but assume the best when people go to work.”
o: Tandon v. Newsom
Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith
Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission
Carson v. Makin
e: From Tandon v. Newsom (2021).
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Tandon v. Newsom

q:
Which case is this from?
An interest in separating church and state more strictly than the federal Constitution requires is not compelling.
o: Carson v. Makin
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District
Tandon v. Newsom
Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith
e: From Carson v. Makin (2022).
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Carson v. Makin

q: How did Congress respond to Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith?
o: It enacted RFRA, restoring strict scrutiny by statute
It proposed a constitutional amendment to overrule Smith
It exempted all sacramental drug use
It removed free exercise cases from federal jurisdiction
e: RFRA (1993) requires strict scrutiny for substantial burdens. City of Boerne v. Flores (1997) held it can’t bind the states; it still binds the federal government.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith

q: Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah illustrates which way a law fails neutrality?
o: Gerrymandered exemptions
A discretionary exemption system
Hostile application
Favoring comparable secular activity
e: Lukumi is the gerrymander case. Masterpiece is hostility, Fulton is discretionary exemptions, and Tandon is favoring comparable secular activity.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah

q: What tension did Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission leave unresolved?
o: Antidiscrimination law versus the First Amendment
The Free Exercise Clause versus the Establishment Clause
Federal versus state power over marriage
Commercial speech versus political speech
e: The Court decided on hostility alone and left the broader conflict between public accommodations law and the First Amendment open. Ginsburg and Sotomayor dissented.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission

q: What did Fulton v. City of Philadelphia decline to do?
o: Overrule Smith’s rule for neutral, generally applicable laws
Apply strict scrutiny to the city’s referral policy
Treat an unused exemption power as relevant to general applicability
Reach the agency’s Free Exercise claim on the merits
e: Fulton decided the case within Smith’s framework. An unused power to grant exemptions still counts.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Fulton v. City of Philadelphia

q: What did the dissent in Tandon v. Newsom say was the right comparator?
o: Secular at-home gatherings, which were treated identically
Retail stores, which the state treated even more strictly than homes
Churches in other states with looser pandemic rules
Outdoor protests, which were not limited at all
e: Kagan’s dissent compared at-home secular gatherings, not salons (“apples and watermelons”), and said the record showed homes are riskier.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Tandon v. Newsom

q: Which two cases complete the funding trilogy with Carson v. Makin?
o: Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia, Inc. v. Comer and Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue
Zelman v. Simmons-Harris and Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board v. Drummond
Lemon v. Kurtzman and Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District and Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah
e: Trinity Lutheran (2017), Espinoza (2020), and Carson (2022) require including religious entities in generally available benefits. Drummond (2025) split 4-4 on religious charter schools.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Carson v. Makin

q: What is the first question on the Free Exercise checklist?
o: Is a sincere religious practice burdened?
Is the religion’s belief logical and widely shared?
Did the statute mention religion in its text?
Is the practice central to the religion’s worship?
e: Beliefs need not be acceptable, logical, consistent, or comprehensible to others (Lukumi). Sincerity is what counts.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — The Free Exercise framework

q: Under Smith, what does a neutral, generally applicable law that incidentally burdens religion get?
o: No exemption; it is valid without strict scrutiny
Strict scrutiny, applied to the requested exemption
Intermediate scrutiny, as with zoning for secondary effects
A balancing test weighing the burden on worship
e: Strict scrutiny for every incidental burden would create “a private right to ignore generally applicable laws.” Congress answered with RFRA.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — The Free Exercise framework

q: What are the elements of strict scrutiny in a Free Exercise case?
o: An interest of the highest order, narrowly tailored, judged as to this claimant
A legitimate interest, rationally related, judged against the law as a whole
An important interest, substantially related, judged across all religions
A compelling interest, pursued by any reasonable means, judged at enactment
e: Fulton framed it as whether the government has a compelling interest in denying this claimant an exemption. The government almost always loses.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — The Free Exercise framework

q: Smith explained earlier exemption cases as “hybrid rights” cases. What did it mean?
o: Free exercise plus another right, like speech or parents’ control of education
The claimant practiced two religions at once, so the burden on belief was doubled
The law regulated religious belief and religious conduct at the same time
Both the federal and the state constitution protected the same practice
e: Yoder paired religion with parental rights, and Barnette was really a speech case. Mahmoud’s Wrinkle 1 grows out of Yoder.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — The Free Exercise framework

q: Even with a neutral law, which of these may government never do?
o: Impose special disabilities based on religious status
Ban a drug that one religion uses in its central rituals
Require all businesses to close on Sundays
Enforce child labor laws against a religious group
e: Smith’s list: no regulating belief, compelling affirmation, punishing doctrines as false, status-based disabilities, or taking sides in religious disputes. The other choices track Smith, Braunfeld, and Prince, where neutral laws were enforced.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — The Free Exercise framework

q: A state bans killing animals outside licensed slaughterhouses. Licenses go to anyone who meets fixed sanitary rules, with no exceptions. A church wants to sacrifice animals in its rituals. What result?
o: No exemption: the law is neutral and generally applicable
Strict scrutiny under Lukumi, because the law burdens a ritual
Strict scrutiny under Fulton, because licensing is discretionary
Rational basis, but only after a finding that the belief is sincere
e: Lukumi failed because its ordinances exempted fishing, hunting, pest control, and euthanasia. An across-the-board rule with fixed criteria looks like Smith’s drug ban.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — The Free Exercise framework

q: A city’s animal-killing ban exempts fishing, hunting, pest control, and euthanasia, but not ritual sacrifice. Which way of failing neutrality is this?
o: Gerrymandered exemptions
Hostility in application
A discretionary exemption system
Exclusion from a public benefit
e: Lukumi. Society imposed on Santeria worshippers what it would not impose on itself; the law was underinclusive for both animal cruelty and public health.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Neutrality and general applicability

q: An official has “sole discretion” to waive a policy but has never granted a waiver. Under Fulton, what follows?
o: The policy isn’t generally applicable; the unused power still counts
The policy stays generally applicable until a waiver is actually granted
The claimant must apply for and be denied a waiver before suing
Only a waiver granted to a secular applicant would trigger scrutiny
e: A formal system of individualized exemptions invites the government to decide which reasons for not complying are worthy.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Neutrality and general applicability

q: Under Tandon, how does a court decide whether a secular activity is “comparable” to religious exercise?
o: By the risk each poses to the government’s interest
By whether each activity takes place in a private home
By how many people each activity typically involves
By whether the legislature named both in the same order
e: The government must show the religious activity is riskier even with the same precautions. The dissent’s comparator was at-home secular gatherings, treated identically.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Neutrality and general applicability

q: Under Tandon, what happens if one comparable secular activity is treated better than worship, while others are treated just as badly?
o: Strict scrutiny applies
Rational basis applies, since most are treated alike
The court averages the treatment of all activities
Intermediate scrutiny applies, as for incidental burdens
e: It doesn’t matter that some secular activities are treated as badly. The state “cannot assume the worst when people go to worship but assume the best when people go to work.”
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Neutrality and general applicability

q: How can a law that is neutral on its face still violate the Free Exercise Clause, as in Masterpiece Cakeshop?
o: Through hostile application, such as officials disparaging the religious objection
Through its legislative history, if any of its sponsors held religious views
Through disparate effects, if religious objectors are fined more often
Through its age, if it was enacted before the religion reached the state
e: Two signs in Masterpiece: commissioners likened religious justification to defenses of slavery and the Holocaust, and three bakers who refused cakes with anti-same-sex-marriage messages were treated better.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Neutrality and general applicability

q: Under the funding cases, when does excluding religious entities from a public benefit trigger strict scrutiny?
o: When they are excluded solely because of their religious character
Only when the benefit is a tax credit rather than a direct cash grant
Only when the excluded entity is a church rather than a school
Only when the money would pay for secular uses, like playgrounds
e: Carson went past Trinity Lutheran (a playground grant): the exclusion fails even when the money pays for religious instruction.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Neutrality and general applicability

q: Which of these does NOT, by itself, make a law fail neutrality or general applicability?
o: It burdens one religion’s ritual more heavily than other faiths
It exempts comparable secular conduct but not the religious conduct
The officials applying it openly disparage the claimant’s faith
Its enforcer may grant individualized exemptions at will
e: A disparate incidental burden is exactly Smith: the drug ban fell hardest on the Native American Church, yet no exemption was required.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Neutrality and general applicability

q: Which way of failing neutrality does Kennedy v. Bremerton School District illustrate?
o: An admitted religious motive
Gerrymandered exemptions for secular speech
A discretionary system of individual waivers
Exclusion from a generally available benefit
e: The district admitted acting partly because the prayer was religious. Its Establishment Clause defense failed because quiet private prayer wasn’t coercion.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Neutrality and general applicability

q: What is Wrinkle 1 in the Free Exercise framework?
o: Strict scrutiny for laws interfering with parents’ religious upbringing of children
Strict scrutiny for any law that burdens worship services held inside a private home
Rational basis for laws that burden religious schools, since attendance is a choice
An automatic exemption from any curriculum a parent finds offensive to the family’s religious faith
e: Yoder and Mahmoud. Smith had grounded Yoder in an unenumerated parental right; wary of such rights after Dobbs, Mahmoud said little about the doctrinal basis.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — The two wrinkles

q: What is Wrinkle 2 in the Free Exercise framework?
o: Government may disfavor religion only when needed to avoid an Establishment Clause violation
Government may disfavor religion whenever its own state constitution demands stricter separation
Government may favor religion only through tax exemptions that are open to all charities
Government may fund religious schools only after a court approves the program in advance
e: Carson: an interest in separating church and state more strictly than the federal Constitution requires is not compelling.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — The two wrinkles

q: Apart from the Yoder-type burden, why did the sex-ed opt-out matter in Mahmoud?
o: It undercut general applicability and the board’s claim that opt-outs were unworkable
It proved that the board had acted out of open hostility toward the parents’ faiths
It showed that the storybooks were legally part of the state-mandated sex-education unit
It meant the parents had waived their claim by using a different opt-out first
e: The board’s administrability problems were, the Court said, of its own design. It also couldn’t cure stigma by stigmatizing religious students.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — The two wrinkles

q: Which of these is broadly agreed to violate the Establishment Clause?
o: Giving tax exemptions only to religious entities
Including religious schools in a neutral voucher program
Opening a legislative session with a short prayer
Keeping a decades-old Ten Commandments monument
e: The agreed core: no official religion, coerced belief, religion-only benefits, favoring a sect, or indoctrination in public schools. Legislative prayer and old monuments survive on history (Van Orden).
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Establishment Clause and funding

q: Why are public schools policed most strictly under the Establishment Clause?
o: They are uniquely coercive and children are impressionable
They receive more public money than any other institution
They are run by elected boards rather than by legislatures
They were the setting of the founding-era establishment fights
e: Engel (nonmandatory prayer), Schempp (Bible reading), Wallace (moment of silence for prayer). Individual religious expression at school is still protected (Kennedy).
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Establishment Clause and funding

q: Under Zelman, when may public money reach religious schools?
o: When it flows through parents’ genuine, independent private choice
Only when it pays for secular subjects like math, science, and reading
Only when religious schools are a minority of eligible schools
Only when the program serves students with disabilities
e: That is “permitted inclusion.” The trilogy moved to “required inclusion”: once the state subsidizes, it can’t exclude religious schools.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Establishment Clause and funding

q: What does the funding trilogy (Trinity Lutheran, Espinoza, Carson) require of a state?
o: If it subsidizes private entities, it can’t exclude religious ones for being religious
It must fund private religious schools whenever its public schools are inadequate
It may exclude religious entities so long as its own constitution requires that
It must give religious schools the same curriculum as its own public schools
e: The escape valve: the state may end the program instead, keep its public schools strictly secular, or not fund private education at all.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Establishment Clause and funding

q: “Play in the joints” had two meanings. Which one survives today?
o: Government may accommodate religion beyond what Free Exercise requires
Government may decline to fund religion to avoid Establishment concerns
Government may prefer one faith if it accommodates all the others too
Government may exclude religion from benefits it isn’t required to give
e: Concept #1 is alive (RFRA, RLUIPA, Cutter). Concept #2 is in retreat; the trilogy rejected it.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Establishment Clause and funding

q: Which approach to the Establishment Clause did Kennedy adopt?
o: History and tradition, with coercion as a core concern
Lemon’s three prongs: purpose, effect, and entanglement
Endorsement: whether a reasonable observer sees approval
Strict separation: no public money or space for religion
e: Kennedy abandoned Lemon and the endorsement test. Coercion takes more than visible religious exercise by a public employee.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Establishment Clause and funding

q: Why do religious charter schools pose a dilemma?
o: If charters are public, religious ones violate the Establishment Clause; if private, excluding them violates Free Exercise
If charters are private, religious ones violate the Establishment Clause; if public, they need no state approval at all
Charters take federal money, so RFRA rather than the Constitution decides which religious schools may open
Charters can’t be religious under federal law, so the issue reaches the Court only on statutory grounds
e: Drummond (2025) split 4-4, leaving in place the state ruling against St. Isidore’s charter. Expect the issue to return.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — Establishment Clause and funding

q: What does the Religious Freedom Restoration Act do?
o: Requires strict scrutiny for substantial burdens on religion, even from neutral laws
Overrules Smith as a matter of constitutional law, binding every level of government
Bars religious exemptions from federal laws unless Congress lists them
Applies rational basis to religious burdens but requires advance notice
e: RFRA (1993) was Congress’s response to Smith. It is a statute, not constitutional law, so Congress can carve exceptions from it.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — RFRA, RLUIPA, and accommodation

q: After City of Boerne v. Flores, whom does RFRA bind?
o: Only the federal government
Only state and local governments
All governments, federal and state
Only employers with fifty or more workers
e: Boerne held RFRA exceeded Congress’s power as to states and localities. RLUIPA, narrower (land use and institutionalized persons), binds states and was upheld in Cutter.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — RFRA, RLUIPA, and accommodation

q: What limit did Cutter v. Wilkinson place on religious accommodation?
o: Courts must weigh the burdens it imposes on nonbeneficiaries
Accommodation is allowed only where Free Exercise requires it
Accommodation must extend equally to secular moral objections
Accommodation is limited to prisons and may not reach land use
e: Cutter warned that “at some point, accommodation may devolve into an unlawful fostering of religion.” Hobby Lobby shows the third-party costs.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — RFRA, RLUIPA, and accommodation

q: What does Burwell v. Hobby Lobby illustrate about religious accommodation?
o: Its costs can fall on third parties, like employees who lose coverage
It extends only to individual believers, never to for-profit corporations
It must come from the Constitution itself rather than from a statute
It covers burdens on worship services but not on running a business
e: RFRA exempted closely held for-profit corporations from the contraceptive mandate. Hobby Lobby alone had 10,000 employees who lost coverage.
topic: Ch. 2 · The Religion Clauses — RFRA, RLUIPA, and accommodation

q:
A state requires its motto “Live Free or Die” on passenger license plates and makes covering it a crime. A Jehovah’s Witness couple tapes over the motto and is fined.
Which case is this?
o: Wooley v. Maynard
West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette
Collin v. Smith
American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut
e: Wooley v. Maynard (1977): The state couldn’t punish drivers for covering the motto.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Wooley v. Maynard

q:
A Nazi party plans a 30-minute sidewalk march, with uniforms and placards, in a village home to thousands of Holocaust survivors. The village passes ordinances to block it.
Which case is this?
o: Collin v. Smith
American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut
Terminiello v. City of Chicago
R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul
e: Collin v. Smith (1978): The ordinances blocking the march were unconstitutional.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Collin v. Smith

q:
A city bans sexually explicit material depicting women as subordinate, for example as enjoying humiliation, regardless of literary or political value. Explicit material treating women as equals stays legal.
Which case is this?
o: American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut
Collin v. Smith
United States v. Stevens
City of Renton v. Playtime Theatres, Inc.
e: American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut (1985): It was unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut

q:
A federal law criminalizes selling depictions of animals being intentionally maimed, tortured, or killed, aimed at “crush videos.” A man is convicted for selling dogfighting videos.
Which case is this?
o: United States v. Stevens
United States v. Alvarez
United States v. Hansen
Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association
e: United States v. Stevens (2010): The ban was substantially overbroad and facially invalid.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Stevens

q:
At a public water-district meeting, a newly elected official falsely claims he received the Medal of Honor. He seeks no money or benefit, but he is prosecuted under the Stolen Valor Act.
Which case is this?
o: United States v. Alvarez
United States v. Stevens
United States v. Hansen
Wooley v. Maynard
e: United States v. Alvarez (2012): The Stolen Valor Act was unconstitutional.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Alvarez

q:
A man defrauds noncitizens with a fake “adult adoption” path to citizenship and is convicted under a law barring “encouraging or inducing” illegal immigration. He argues it is overbroad because it reaches advocacy.
Which case is this?
o: United States v. Hansen
United States v. Stevens
United States v. Williams
United States v. Alvarez
e: United States v. Hansen (2023): The encourage-or-induce law was not facially overbroad.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Hansen

q: What did Wooley v. Maynard hold?
o: The state couldn’t punish drivers for covering the motto
The motto was government speech drivers had to display
Drivers could cover it only for a religious objection
The rule was valid as a vehicle identification measure for police
e: No one can be made a courier for the state’s ideological message on private property. Passive display counts.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Wooley v. Maynard

q: What did Collin v. Smith hold?
o: The ordinances blocking the march were unconstitutional
The march could be banned as fighting words aimed at survivors
The survivors were a captive audience the village could protect
The march had to avoid residential streets
e: The ordinances were content-based, not time, place, or manner rules: the village objected to who was marching.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Collin v. Smith

q: What did American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut hold?
o: It was unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination
The material was obscene, so the ban stood
The city failed to show that the material caused any harm
The ordinance was a valid zoning rule for adult businesses
e: Material treating women as equals was lawful; material treating them as subordinate was banned regardless of value. That is viewpoint discrimination.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut

q: What did United States v. Stevens hold?
o: The ban was substantially overbroad and facially invalid
Depictions of animal cruelty are a new unprotected category
The law was valid as applied to the dogfighting videos
The law survived because of its serious-value exception
e: Read by its text, the law reached hunting videos; lawful applications dwarfed the crush and dogfight market.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Stevens

q: What did United States v. Alvarez hold?
o: The Stolen Valor Act was unconstitutional
False statements of fact are always unprotected
The Act was valid to protect the Medal’s integrity
The Act was valid as applied to public meetings
e: There is no general falsity exception. Unprotected falsehoods, like defamation and fraud, involve legally cognizable harm.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Alvarez

q: What did United States v. Hansen hold?
o: The encourage-or-induce law was not facially overbroad
The law was overbroad because it reached political advocacy
The law was void for vagueness under the Due Process Clause
Hansen’s scheme was protected speech about immigration
e: Read as criminal-law terms of art, the law covers only intentional solicitation and facilitation of specific unlawful acts.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Hansen

q:
Which case stands for this rule?
The state may not require a person to display its ideological message on private property for the public to see; the rights to speak and not to speak are complementary.
o: Wooley v. Maynard
Collin v. Smith
American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut
Cohen v. California
e: Wooley v. Maynard (1977). No one can be made a courier for the state’s ideological message on private property. Passive display counts.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Wooley v. Maynard

q:
Which case stands for this rule?
Government may not ban a peaceful demonstration because of its message, even one that deeply offends or traumatizes listeners.
o: Collin v. Smith
Terminiello v. City of Chicago
R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul
Cohen v. California
e: Collin v. Smith (1978). The ordinances were content-based, not time, place, or manner rules: the village objected to who was marching.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Collin v. Smith

q:
Which case stands for this rule?
Government may not favor one viewpoint and silence the other, even when it is right that the disfavored speech causes real social harm.
o: American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut
United States v. Stevens
City of Renton v. Playtime Theatres, Inc.
New York v. Ferber
e: American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut (1985). Material treating women as equals was lawful; material treating them as subordinate was banned regardless of value. That is viewpoint discrimination.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut

q:
Which case stands for this rule?
Content-based restrictions are presumptively invalid unless the speech falls in a historically unprotected category, and courts may not create new categories by balancing value against costs.
o: United States v. Stevens
United States v. Hansen
Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association
New York v. Ferber
e: United States v. Stevens (2010). Read by its text, the law reached hunting videos; lawful applications dwarfed the crush and dogfight market.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Stevens

q:
Which case stands for this rule?
There is no general First Amendment exception for false statements; a content-based ban on lies must be “actually necessary,” and the remedy for false speech is true speech.
o: United States v. Alvarez
United States v. Hansen
Wooley v. Maynard
Counterman v. Colorado
e: United States v. Alvarez (2012). There is no general falsity exception. Unprotected falsehoods, like defamation and fraud, involve legally cognizable harm.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Alvarez

q:
Which case stands for this rule?
A law is facially overbroad only if it prohibits a substantial amount of protected speech relative to its plainly legitimate sweep: realistic applications and a lopsided ratio.
o: United States v. Hansen
United States v. Williams
United States v. Alvarez
Rice v. Paladin Enterprises, Inc.
e: United States v. Hansen (2023). Read as criminal-law terms of art, the law covers only intentional solicitation and facilitation of specific unlawful acts.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Hansen

q: Why did vehicle identification fail to justify the motto requirement in Wooley v. Maynard?
o: Plate numbers already identify cars, so it wasn’t narrowly tailored
Identifying vehicles is not a legitimate interest of the state
Police had stopped using license plates to identify cars
The state admitted it never used the motto for anything
e: Plate numbers do the identifying. Promoting state pride is an ideological interest that can’t outweigh the right not to be its courier.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Wooley v. Maynard

q: Why did Collin v. Smith reject the village’s captive-audience argument?
o: Residents could avoid Village Hall for the half hour
Captive-audience protection covers only schoolchildren
The march was scheduled for an early weekend morning
The village had never passed a formal noise ordinance
e: Listener protection is limited to intrusions into the home or a truly captive audience.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Collin v. Smith

q: How did American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut treat the claim that such material perpetuates subordination?
o: It accepted the harm, which only showed the power of speech
It rejected the claim as unsupported by any evidence
It held that harm to women isn’t a legitimate interest
It sent the question back for a jury to decide on remand
e: The court accepted the premise; that only shows speech’s power, as with Hitler, communism, religion, and television.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut

q: Why didn’t the government’s promise to prosecute only “extreme” cruelty save the law in United States v. Stevens?
o: Courts won’t uphold a law based on promised prosecutorial restraint
The government had already prosecuted sellers of hunting videos
The promise was made only in the lower courts, not the Supreme Court
Extreme cruelty is itself a fully protected subject of speech
e: The First Amendment doesn’t leave us “at the mercy of noblesse oblige.” Alito dissented, reading the statute narrowly.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Stevens

q: In United States v. Alvarez, what showed that counterspeech worked?
o: Alvarez was exposed and ridiculed for the lie
A court ordered a retraction
The water district voted to remove Alvarez from office
Veterans’ groups won a defamation suit against Alvarez
e: Counterspeech exposed him: the marketplace of ideas (Holmes, Abrams). There was also no evidence the lie diluted the Medal.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Alvarez

q: How did United States v. Hansen read “encourage or induce”?
o: As terms of art for intentional solicitation and facilitation
In their ordinary sense, reaching general public advocacy of all kinds
As limited to speech made for commercial profit
As covering only statements to government officials
e: Constitutional avoidance: adopt any fairly possible constitutional reading, though the canon can’t override clear text.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Hansen

q: Which facts belong to Wooley v. Maynard?
o: Drivers fined for covering “Live Free or Die” on their license plates.
Jehovah’s Witness children expelled for refusing a mandatory flag salute and Pledge.
A city ordinance banning explicit material that depicts women as subordinate.
A prosecution for falsely claiming the Medal of Honor at a public meeting.
e: Wooley v. Maynard (1977): Drivers fined for covering “Live Free or Die” on their license plates.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Wooley v. Maynard

q: Which facts belong to Collin v. Smith?
o: A village blocks a Nazi march planned where thousands of Holocaust survivors live.
A city ordinance banning explicit material that depicts women as subordinate.
A cross burned in a Black family’s yard, charged under a bias-based fighting-words ordinance.
A filmed Klan rally prosecuted under Ohio’s criminal syndicalism law.
e: Collin v. Smith (1978): A village blocks a Nazi march planned where thousands of Holocaust survivors live.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Collin v. Smith

q: Which facts belong to American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut?
o: A city ordinance banning explicit material that depicts women as subordinate.
A village blocks a Nazi march planned where thousands of Holocaust survivors live.
Zoning that confines adult movie theaters to limited areas of a city.
A prosecution for falsely claiming the Medal of Honor at a public meeting.
e: American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut (1985): A city ordinance banning explicit material that depicts women as subordinate.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut

q: Which facts belong to United States v. Stevens?
o: A conviction for selling dogfighting videos under a ban on depictions of animal cruelty.
A prosecution for falsely claiming the Medal of Honor at a public meeting.
A ban on selling or renting violent video games to minors.
A city ordinance banning explicit material that depicts women as subordinate.
e: United States v. Stevens (2010): A conviction for selling dogfighting videos under a ban on depictions of animal cruelty.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Stevens

q: Which facts belong to United States v. Alvarez?
o: A prosecution for falsely claiming the Medal of Honor at a public meeting.
A conviction for selling dogfighting videos under a ban on depictions of animal cruelty.
Drivers fined for covering “Live Free or Die” on their license plates.
A challenge to the federal ban on pandering or soliciting child pornography.
e: United States v. Alvarez (2012): A prosecution for falsely claiming the Medal of Honor at a public meeting.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Alvarez

q: Which facts belong to United States v. Hansen?
o: An “adult adoption” fraud prosecuted under a ban on encouraging or inducing illegal immigration.
A conviction for selling dogfighting videos under a ban on depictions of animal cruelty.
A prosecution for falsely claiming the Medal of Honor at a public meeting.
Hundreds of unwanted Facebook messages to a musician, prosecuted under an objective-test stalking law.
e: United States v. Hansen (2023): An “adult adoption” fraud prosecuted under a ban on encouraging or inducing illegal immigration.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Hansen

q:
Which case is this from?
Footnote 15 distinguishes “In God We Trust” on currency, which is carried privately and isn’t associated with its bearer.
o: Wooley v. Maynard
American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut
Cohen v. California
United States v. Alvarez
e: From Wooley v. Maynard (1977).
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Wooley v. Maynard

q:
Which case is this from?
Judges may not engage in “ideological tyranny” any more than legislators; protecting unpopular minorities distinguishes the U.S. from the Third Reich.
o: Collin v. Smith
R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul
Cohen v. California
Brandenburg v. Ohio
e: From Collin v. Smith (1978).
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Collin v. Smith

q:
Which case is this from?
Otherwise government becomes “the great censor and director of which thoughts are good for us.”
o: American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut
City of Renton v. Playtime Theatres, Inc.
New York v. Ferber
United States v. Alvarez
e: From American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut (1985).
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut

q:
Which case is this from?
The government’s “categorical balancing” test is “startling and dangerous,” and we aren’t left “at the mercy of noblesse oblige.”
o: United States v. Stevens
Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association
New York v. Ferber
American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut
e: From United States v. Stevens (2010).
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Stevens

q:
Which case is this from?
The law targeted “falsity and nothing more” and reached lies anywhere, even whispered at home.
o: United States v. Alvarez
Wooley v. Maynard
Counterman v. Colorado
United States v. Williams
e: From United States v. Alvarez (2012).
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Alvarez

q:
Which case is this from?
Overbreadth is “strong medicine,” and courts seek harmony, not “constitutional collision.”
o: United States v. Hansen
United States v. Alvarez
Rice v. Paladin Enterprises, Inc.
Counterman v. Colorado
e: From United States v. Hansen (2023).
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Hansen

q: Which compelled-speech case did Wooley v. Maynard extend from flag salutes to passive display?
o: West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District
Minersville School District v. Gobitis
Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith
e: Carrying a motto is less than saluting a flag, but the difference is “one of degree”; the car becomes a “mobile billboard.”
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Wooley v. Maynard

q: Which case did Collin v. Smith rely on for the idea that speech stirring anger serves a high purpose?
o: Terminiello v. City of Chicago
Brandenburg v. Ohio
American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut
R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul
e: Psychic trauma is indistinguishable from speech that stirs anger (Terminiello); debate must be “uninhibited, robust, and wide-open” (New York Times Co. v. Sullivan).
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Collin v. Smith

q: Which test did the ordinance in American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut ignore?
o: Miller v. California’s obscenity test
Brandenburg v. Ohio’s incitement test
Renton’s secondary-effects test
Counterman v. Colorado’s recklessness test
e: No prurient interest, community standards, work-as-a-whole, or value inquiry. Its drafters saw those omissions as virtues; the court saw viewpoint discrimination.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — American Booksellers Ass’n v. Hudnut

q: What did United States v. Stevens leave open?
o: A statute limited to crush videos or extreme cruelty
Whether videos count as speech under the First Amendment
Whether overbreadth doctrine applies to federal statutes
Whether hunting videos are speech
e: Stevens left open a narrower statute. Congress’s 2010 crush-video law was limited to obscene videos.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Stevens

q: What standard did Breyer and Kagan apply in United States v. Alvarez?
o: Intermediate scrutiny, concurring in the judgment
Strict scrutiny, joining the plurality opinion
Rational basis review, in dissent
Exacting scrutiny, writing for a majority of the Court
e: A plurality’s reasoning usually isn’t binding; “concurring in the judgment” means agreeing only with the result. Alito, Scalia, and Thomas dissented.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Alvarez

q: How does United States v. Hansen contrast with United States v. Stevens?
o: Stevens used ordinary meaning; Hansen read terms of art
Stevens applied vagueness; Hansen applied strict scrutiny
Stevens involved a state law; Hansen a federal one
Stevens upheld its statute; Hansen struck its statute
e: Stevens: ordinary meaning, realistic protected applications, facially invalid. Hansen: terms of art, fanciful concerns, upheld. Ordinary facial challenges need no valid applications (Salerno).
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — United States v. Hansen

q: Which is the best statement of what counts as “speech” under the First Amendment?
o: Words, images, and symbolic acts like armbands, flags, and picketing
Spoken and written words, with all conduct left to the states
Words and images, plus conduct only when it is used at an organized protest
Political words and images, but not entertainment like games
e: Barnette treated the salute as “a form of utterance,” Collin treated uniforms and marching as speech, and Brown treated video games as speech.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Speech Clause principles

q: Why does the Court prefer bright-line rules over balancing standards in speech cases?
o: Distrust: officials can’t be trusted to sort valuable speech from harmful speech
Efficiency: bright lines are cheaper for trial courts to administer quickly
Text: the First Amendment is phrased in absolute terms the Court must follow
Deference: legislatures can draft precise rules that courts can enforce
e: The same distrust explains why false, heinous, and harmful speech is often protected, and why the Court refuses to add unprotected categories.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Speech Clause principles

q: What is “chilling,” and which doctrines counter it?
o: Self-censorship from fear of liability; overbreadth and mens rea requirements
Delay in granting parade permits; the presumption against prior restraints on speech
Listeners tuning out offensive speech; the captive-audience doctrine
Speakers lying to avoid prosecution; the rule against false statements
e: Counterman’s recklessness requirement and Stevens’s overbreadth holding both rest on the fear of chilling honest speakers.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Speech Clause principles

q: What is the right order for the first four steps of the speech checklist?
o: Government action, speech, compelled speech, content-based or neutral
Content-based or viewpoint-based, government action, speech, compelled speech
Speech, unprotected category, government action, strict scrutiny
Strict scrutiny, unprotected category, government action, speech
e: Next: does it fall in a narrowly defined historical category? If not and it’s content-based, strict scrutiny. Facial attacks (overbreadth, vagueness) come last.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Speech Clause principles

q: At the strict-scrutiny step of the speech checklist, what must the government show?
o: A compelling interest, a law “actually necessary” to it, and the least restrictive means
A substantial interest, a reasonable fit, and ample alternative channels for the same speech
A legitimate interest and some rational connection between the law and that interest
An important interest unrelated to suppressing speech, burdening no more than needed
e: Counterspeech is often the less restrictive alternative (Alvarez). The last two choices describe rational basis and intermediate scrutiny.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Speech Clause principles

q: What is the main exception to the near-ban on compelled speech?
o: Compelled commercial disclosures, like nutrition labels
Patriotic exercises for public school students
State mottos on government-issued property, like license plates
Statements of belief by public employees
e: The right to speak includes the right not to speak. Compelled commercial disclosures (nutrition labels, drug side effects) are Ch. 8 material.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Compelled speech

q: Why is “In God We Trust” on currency treated differently from “Live Free or Die” on a license plate?
o: Currency is carried privately and isn’t associated with the bearer
Currency carries a religious motto that the Establishment Clause allows
The currency motto was adopted by Congress rather than a state legislature
No one has ever been prosecuted for covering the motto on money
e: Wooley’s footnote 15. Circuits have upheld the currency motto (Newdow v. Peterson).
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Compelled speech

q: Does it matter to a compelled-speech claim that most people approve of the message?
o: No; majority approval is irrelevant
Yes; popular messages may be compelled after a public vote
Yes; only messages most people reject are protected
No, but only because the objectors were religious
e: Barnette: fundamental rights “depend on the outcome of no elections.” Wooley’s plaintiffs were Jehovah’s Witnesses, but its speech rationale protects any objector.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Compelled speech

q: Why did Wooley treat passively displaying a motto like reciting a pledge?
o: The difference is one of degree; the car becomes a mobile billboard
Displaying a motto is more intrusive than saying it aloud once
The motto was religious, so the Free Exercise Clause applied
Drivers had no other practical way to identify their vehicles on the road
e: Driving is a virtual necessity, so the state forced drivers to carry its ideological message. Plate numbers already serve identification, so that interest wasn’t narrowly tailored.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Compelled speech

q: Classify this rule: “No speeches about sports teams in the park.”
o: Content-based: strict scrutiny
Viewpoint-based: per se invalid
Content-neutral: intermediate scrutiny
Unprotected category: rational basis
e: It turns on subject matter but not on side. Banning only pro-legalization publications would be viewpoint-based, the worst form.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Content, viewpoint, and scrutiny

q: Classify this rule: “No amplified speeches between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.”
o: Content-neutral: intermediate scrutiny
Content-based: strict scrutiny
Viewpoint-based: strict scrutiny
Prior restraint: heavy presumption of invalidity
e: Time, place, and manner rules come in Ch. 9. Collin rejected the TPM label because the village objected to who was marching, not when or where.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Content, viewpoint, and scrutiny

q: A state rejects the vanity plate “FCANCER” while allowing other vanity plates. What kind of restriction is this?
o: Viewpoint-based, the worst form of content regulation
Content-neutral, because every vanity plate is screened
A permissible ban within the fighting-words category
A valid ban on profanity, which is unprotected speech
e: The cancer survivor won in district court in 2024. Calling speech profane doesn’t make it restrictable (Cohen).
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Content, viewpoint, and scrutiny

q: Under Collin, when may government protect listeners from offensive speech?
o: Only for intrusions into the home or on a truly captive audience
Whenever the speech causes listeners measurable psychic trauma or distress
Whenever most of the community finds the message hateful
Whenever the speech targets a religious or ethnic minority
e: Skokie residents could avoid Village Hall for half an hour. Psychic trauma is indistinguishable from speech that stirs anger, a high purpose of speech (Terminiello).
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Content, viewpoint, and scrutiny

q: Hudnut accepted that the banned depictions perpetuate women’s subordination. Why did the ordinance still fail?
o: Harm through ideas only shows speech’s power; government can’t pick a side
The harm was speculative, so the city failed the compelling-interest prong of strict scrutiny
The ordinance was drafted by activists, not by the city’s own legislature
The harm fell on adults, and only harm to children can justify a ban
e: Otherwise government becomes “the great censor.” Because it ignored Miller’s elements, it couldn’t be saved as an obscenity law either.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Content, viewpoint, and scrutiny

q: What level of review applies to each kind of speech restriction?
o: Strict for content- and viewpoint-based laws; intermediate for content-neutral; rational basis inside unprotected categories
Strict for viewpoint-based laws only; intermediate for content-based; rational basis for content-neutral laws
Strict for every speech restriction; intermediate only for commercial speech; rational basis for none
Strict for prior restraints only; intermediate for content-based laws; rational basis for all other laws
e: Content-based laws are presumptively invalid. R.A.V. still limits regulation inside a category: no topic or viewpoint subsets.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Content, viewpoint, and scrutiny

q: Which of these is NOT a historically unprotected category of speech?
o: Depictions of animal cruelty
Speech integral to criminal conduct
True threats
Fighting words
e: Stevens refused to add it, and Alvarez refused to add false statements as such. The list: incitement, fighting words, grave and imminent threats, true threats, speech integral to crime, child pornography, obscenity, defamation, and fraud.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Unprotected categories

q: May courts create a new unprotected category by weighing a kind of speech’s value against its social costs?
o: No; Stevens called that test startling and dangerous
Yes, if the speech’s value is shown to be de minimis or nearly so
Yes, but only for speech directed at minors
No; only Congress may add categories, by statute
e: Describing unprotected speech as “low-value” is descriptive, not a test; the First Amendment already reflects the people’s cost-benefit judgment. Brown applied this to violence for minors.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Unprotected categories

q: Why is there no general First Amendment exception for false statements?
o: Cases calling falsehood valueless involved legally cognizable harm, like fraud
False statements always carry literary or political value worth protecting
The Framers protected lies expressly in the debates over the Bill of Rights
Only the states, not Congress, may punish lies, and the states haven’t tried
e: Alvarez: the Stolen Valor Act targeted “falsity and nothing more.” Upholding it would let government list subjects about which lies are crimes.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Unprotected categories

q: If speech falls within an unprotected category, what review does a ban on it get?
o: Rational basis, subject to R.A.V.’s bar on singling out subsets
Strict scrutiny, because the ban is still content-based on its face
Intermediate scrutiny, as with secondary-effects zoning
None, because the category is invisible to the Constitution
e: R.A.V.: categories aren’t “invisible to the Constitution.” Government may ban libel, but not only libel critical of the government.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Unprotected categories

q: Match the category to its key case: speech integral to criminal conduct.
o: Giboney v. Empire Storage & Ice Co.
Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire
Watts v. United States
Miller v. California
e: Chaplinsky is fighting words, Watts is true threats, and Miller is obscenity. Williams and Paladin build on Giboney.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Unprotected categories

q: What must a challenger show to win an overbreadth claim?
o: The law reaches a substantial amount of protected speech relative to its legitimate sweep
The law has at least one protected application, whether realistic or merely hypothetical
The law has no valid applications at all, as in an ordinary facial challenge
The law uses terms that fail to give a person of ordinary intelligence fair notice
e: Hansen: the unconstitutional applications must be realistic and the ratio lopsided. Overbreadth is “strong medicine.”
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Overbreadth and narrowing

q: What is unusual about who may bring an overbreadth challenge?
o: A litigant whose own speech is unprotected may assert others’ rights
Only a litigant whose own speech is protected may bring the claim
Only the government may raise it, to narrow its own statute
Only a speaker who has already been prosecuted under the statute may sue
e: Justified by chilling: people the law covers might self-censor instead of suing. It also invalidates a law that has lawful applications.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Overbreadth and narrowing

q: Before declaring a statute overbroad, what must a court do first?
o: Construe it, adopting any fairly possible constitutional reading
Sever every clause that could ever reach protected speech
Give the legislature a chance to amend the statute before ruling on it
Find that the defendant’s own speech was protected
e: Constitutional avoidance (Ashwander). The canon can’t override clear text, which is why Stevens read § 48 by its ordinary meaning.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Overbreadth and narrowing

q: Why was § 48 struck down in Stevens while the statute in Hansen was upheld?
o: Stevens’s protected uses were realistic and many; Hansen’s were fanciful once narrowed
Stevens involved a federal law, while Hansen involved a state law with a severability clause
Stevens’s own speech was protected, while Hansen’s own speech was unprotected fraud
Stevens applied strict scrutiny, while Hansen applied only intermediate scrutiny
e: Hunting videos made § 48’s ratio lopsided. Reading “encourage or induce” as solicitation and facilitation excluded advocacy, leaving only fanciful concerns.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Overbreadth and narrowing

q: What does an ordinary facial challenge (outside overbreadth) require?
o: No valid applications (Salerno)
A substantial number of invalid applications
One invalid application to the litigant
Proof that the law chills some speech
e: Overbreadth relaxes Salerno for speech cases, because waiting for as-applied challenges would let the law chill speech in the meantime.
topic: Ch. 3 · Speech Clause Overview — Overbreadth and narrowing

q:
A suspended priest gives a hate-filled speech to a packed auditorium while protesters gather outside. The jury is told breach of the peace includes speech that “stirs the public to anger” or “invites dispute.”
Which case is this?
o: Terminiello v. City of Chicago
Brandenburg v. Ohio
Cohen v. California
Collin v. Smith
e: Terminiello v. City of Chicago (1949): The conviction was reversed because the instruction reached protected speech.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Terminiello v. City of Chicago

q:
A KKK leader invites a reporter to film a farm rally. Hooded figures, some armed, burn a cross; he warns of possible “revengeance” and announces a march on Congress. He is convicted under a criminal syndicalism law.
Which case is this?
o: Brandenburg v. Ohio
Terminiello v. City of Chicago
Whitney v. California
Counterman v. Colorado
e: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969): Ohio’s criminal syndicalism law was unconstitutional.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Brandenburg v. Ohio

q:
Teenagers burn a cross in a Black family’s fenced yard. They are charged under a city ordinance banning symbols that arouse anger “on the basis of race, color, creed, religion or gender,” construed to reach only fighting words.
Which case is this?
o: R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul
Cohen v. California
Terminiello v. City of Chicago
Collin v. Smith
e: R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul (1992): The ordinance was facially invalid for singling out some fighting words.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul

q:
State courts enjoin a newspaper from publishing articles accusing local law enforcement officials of corruption.
Which case is this?
o: Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson
New York Times Co. v. United States
Terminiello v. City of Chicago
Brandenburg v. Ohio
e: Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson (1931): The injunction was an invalid prior restraint.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson

q:
A leaker gives newspapers a classified Vietnam War study showing the government knew the war likely couldn’t be won. The Administration seeks to enjoin publication, which is restrained for 15 days.
Which case is this?
o: New York Times Co. v. United States
Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson
Brandenburg v. Ohio
Terminiello v. City of Chicago
e: New York Times Co. v. United States (1971): The injunctions were denied; the government didn’t meet its burden.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — New York Times Co. v. United States

q: What did Terminiello v. City of Chicago hold?
o: The conviction was reversed because the instruction reached protected speech
The conviction stood because the speech was incitement to riot
The speech was fighting words aimed directly at the protesters
The city could punish any speech that caused a public disturbance
e: Speech can’t be punished merely for stirring anger or creating unrest.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Terminiello v. City of Chicago

q: What did Brandenburg v. Ohio hold?
o: Ohio’s criminal syndicalism law was unconstitutional
The conviction stood under the clear and present danger test
Klan rallies are unprotected fighting words
The law was valid but misapplied to this speaker
e: The law punished mere advocacy, with no intent, imminence, or likelihood requirement. It overruled Whitney v. California.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Brandenburg v. Ohio

q: What did R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul hold?
o: The ordinance was facially invalid for singling out some fighting words
Cross burning is protected because it can never be fighting words
The ordinance was valid because it reached only fighting words
The teenagers’ conduct could not be punished under any law
e: Even within fighting words, St. Paul couldn’t pick out race, religion, and gender.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul

q: What did Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson hold?
o: The injunction was an invalid prior restraint
The paper could be enjoined for defaming officials
The paper had to prove its charges before printing
States may license papers covering public officials
e: Reversed: a prior restraint stops speech before it occurs, which the Framers especially opposed.
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson

q: What did New York Times Co. v. United States hold?
o: The injunctions were denied; the government didn’t meet its burden
Classified material is unprotected once the nation is at war
The papers could publish only after redacting troop details
The executive’s judgment of security harm is conclusive
e: The Pentagon Papers case. Don’t confuse it with New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (defamation).
topic: Ch. 4 · Violence and National Security — New York Times Co. v. United States

q:
Which case stands for this rule?
Speech may not be punished for stirring anger or inviting dispute; it must pose a clear and present danger of a serious evil far above public inconvenience or annoyance.
